# From Entropy-Based Learning to the Free-Energy Principle {#sec-fep}

The free-energy principle (FEP) is the most ambitious claim in this
neighbourhood of ideas: that perception, learning, action, and — in its
strongest form — the persistence of living things are all one optimization.
It was developed in theoretical neuroscience, largely by Friston and
collaborators [@friston2005theory; @friston2006free; @friston2010free], and
it is usually presented in a vocabulary of its own. 
This chapter examines the connection of the free-energy principle in the terms and concepts developed throughout this book.
Some of the FEP is an
identity with material we have already derived: it is @eq-max-def-free at
$T = 1$, read in a particular way. Some of it is a correspondence, close
enough to be illuminating but not a theorem. 
Other aspects — such as the physics of Markov blankets and non-equilibrium steady states — stand apart from the framework developed in this book, and we will make that distinction clear.


The reason to spend a chapter on this is not completeness. It is that the
FEP supplies the one ingredient the preceding chapters leave implicit.
Chapters 5 through 7 organize methods as an inner free-energy problem under
an outer criterion, and that criterion either fits the data (@sec-max-entropy), or sharpens the model's own output (@sec-min-entropy), or
chooses which features to measure and which assignments to commit to (@sec-minimax-entropy). All three take the data as given. Active inference
does not: its outer problem chooses *what to observe*. 
We propose that this constitutes a third distinct type of outer problem, as described in @sec-minimax-two-questions—precisely the kind that has been absent from the rest of the book. Making this explicit serves to clarify the structure and implications on both fronts.


Because the principle will be unfamiliar to many readers of this book, the
chapter is arranged in four parts. The first, @sec-fep-foundations, presents
the FEP on its own terms and in its own notation — where it came from, what
it says about perception, learning, and action, and the physical claims that
were later built on it — with two worked examples, of perception and of
planning. The second, @sec-fep-recent, surveys the developments of the field
since 2019, critiques included. 
The third section, @sec-fep-connections, acts as a bridge: it clarifies which aspects of the free-energy principle are mathematically identical to the free energy discussed in @sec-free-energy, which aspects are related but only by analogy, and which fall outside both categories. To illustrate these connections, it adds two additional examples—one focused on learning processes, and another on the case where preferences themselves are subject to learning.
The fourth, @sec-fep-takeaway, collects what the translation establishes
and what it leaves open. The numbers in all four examples come from
`code/fep-examples.py`.

## Foundations of the free-energy principle {#sec-fep-foundations}

### Origins {#sec-fep-origins}

The idea behind the FEP is older than the name. Helmholtz described
perception as *unconscious inference* about the causes of sensations, and
the FEP begins by taking that description literally [@friston2005theory].
Its direct predecessors in machine learning are the Helmholtz machine
[@dayan1995helmholtz] and the free-energy view of EM [@neal1998em], both of
which read the evidence lower bound as a negative variational free energy, as
the table of @sec-free-energy records. What Friston, a neuroscientist at
University College London, added was the claim that the brain — and, later,
any system that persists — minimizes this quantity, and that perception,
learning, and action are the three ways of doing so.

The principle took shape in roughly four steps. i) In 2005, Friston observed
that perceptual inference and perceptual learning both rest on minimizing the
brain's free energy, with learning arising from synaptic changes that
minimize the free energy averaged over the stimuli encountered
[@friston2005theory]; in 2006, with Kilner and Harrison, he termed this a
free-energy principle for the brain [@friston2006free]. ii) In 2007, the
variational Laplace method gave a practical algorithm for computing the free
energy under a Gaussian approximation [@friston2007laplace]. iii) Two reviews
of 2009–2010 promoted it to a unified brain theory [@friston2009rough; @friston2010free], and "Action and behavior" of 2010 brought in action,
reading motor control as the fulfilment of prior expectations about
proprioceptive sensations [@friston2010action]. iv) From 2012 on, *active
inference* on discrete state spaces recast optimal control as a pure
inference problem, with cost functions absorbed into prior beliefs about
state transitions and terminal states [@friston2012agency]; it then
introduced the expected free energy and epistemic value
[@friston2015epistemic], learning and habits [@friston2016learning], and a
process theory for the brain [@friston2017process]. The textbook is *Active
Inference* by Parr, Pezzulo, and Friston [@parr2022active]; a mathematical
review is that of Buckley et al. [@buckley2017review], and an introductory
tutorial is that of Bogacz [@bogacz2017tutorial], whose running example we
adopt below.

In outline, the principle says the following. A system that persists must
keep its sensory exchanges with the environment within bounds, i.e., it must
avoid surprising sensations, where the surprise of an observation $o$ under
a model is $-\log p(o)$. Surprise cannot be evaluated directly, because the
model has hidden causes that would have to be integrated out, so the system
minimizes a tractable upper bound on it, the *variational free energy*. It
has three ways of doing so: it can change its beliefs about the causes,
which is perception; it can change the model, which is learning; or it can
change the sensations themselves by acting on the world, which is action.
The quantities behind these three sentences are developed in the next four
subsections; the physical claim that makes "persists" into a theorem, by way
of Markov blankets and steady states, is set out in @sec-fep-blankets.

### Variational free energy and perception {#sec-fep-vfe}

The FEP starts from a *generative model*, namely a joint distribution
$p(o, s) = p(s)\, p(o \mid s)$ over observations $o$ and their hidden causes
$s$, which the agent is assumed to embody. Given an observation, the agent
cannot in general compute the posterior $p(s \mid o)$ or the evidence
$p(o)$, so it maintains an approximate belief $q(s)$, termed the recognition
density, and scores it by the variational free energy

$$
\begin{aligned}
F[q; o] \;&=\; \mathbb{E}_{q(s)}\big[-\log p(o, s)\big] - H[q] \\
&=\; \mathrm{KL}\big(q(s) \,\Vert\, p(s \mid o)\big) - \log p(o) \\
&=\; \underbrace{\mathrm{KL}\big(q(s) \,\Vert\, p(s)\big)}_{\text{complexity}}
\;-\; \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q(s)}\big[\log p(o \mid s)\big]}_{\text{accuracy}}
\;\;\ge\;\; -\log p(o) .
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-fep-vfe}

The three lines read "energy minus entropy", "divergence plus surprise", and
"complexity minus accuracy". The second shows that $F$ is an upper bound on
the surprise $-\log p(o)$, with equality if and only if $q$ is the exact
posterior, so that minimizing $F$ does two things at once: it brings $q$ to
the posterior, which is perception, and it brings $F$ down to the surprise,
which gives a computable bound on the model evidence — the negative of the
evidence lower bound of @sec-free-energy. We note at once that what the FEP
minimizes is the surprise of particular observations and not an entropy; the
two are linked by a sentence of Friston's — under ergodic assumptions, the
long-term average of surprise is entropy [@friston2013life] — to which we
return in @sec-fep-blankets and @sec-fep-duality.

**Example 1 (perception).** We take the example of Bogacz's tutorial
[@bogacz2017tutorial]: an animal infers the size $v$ of a food item from an
observed light intensity $u$, with the prior $v \sim \mathcal{N}(3, 1)$, the
likelihood $u \mid v \sim \mathcal{N}(v^2, 1)$, and the observation $u = 2$.
The model is nonlinear and the posterior has no closed form, but in one
dimension it can be computed on a fine grid. The surprise is
$-\log p(u) = 3.2368$ nats, and the posterior has mean $1.4797$, standard
deviation $0.3425$, and mode $1.5675$. Gradient descent on @eq-fep-vfe over
the Gaussian family $q = \mathcal{N}(m, s^2)$, started at the prior,
converges to $m^\star = 1.4933$ and $s^\star = 0.3025$ with
$F^\star = 3.2636$. The excess of $F^\star$ over the surprise, $0.026828$
nats, agrees with $\mathrm{KL}(q^\star \Vert p(v \mid u))$ to within
$10^{-13}$, as the second line of @eq-fep-vfe says it must. At the starting
point the free energy is $51.92$ nats, since the prior predicts an intensity
$v^2 \approx 9$, far from the observed value 2 (@fig-fep-perception a, b).

![Perception as free-energy minimization (Example 1). (a) Prior, normalized likelihood, exact posterior, the best Gaussian $q^\star$, and the Laplace approximation after observing $u = 2$, with the posterior mode marked; (b) the excess of $F(q)$ over the surprise along gradient descent, converging to $\mathrm{KL}(q^\star \Vert p(v \mid u)) = 0.0268$; (c) the predictive-coding network, whose state $\phi$ and two error nodes converge to their values at the posterior mode. Produced by `code/fep-examples.py`.](../figures/fep-perception.png){#fig-fep-perception width="100%"}

### Predictive coding, precision, and attention {#sec-fep-pc}

*Predictive coding* is the process theory that implements the minimization
in neural tissue, as message passing between units that carry states and
units that carry prediction errors [@rao1999predictive; @friston2005theory].
The name is older than the principle, and the idea is best seen where it
started. In the engineering of signals, Elias proposed to transmit not a
signal but the difference between the signal and a prediction of it formed
from its own past: the difference is smaller and cheaper to send, and a
receiver that forms the same prediction loses nothing
[@elias1955predictive]. The channel is then quiet as long as the world
behaves as expected and speaks only when something unpredicted happens, as
in @fig-fep-predictive-coding (c). Srinivasan, Laughlin, and Dubs read the
centre–surround organization of early visual neurons in the same way: the
surround forms a prediction of the centre from its neighbours, the cell
transmits the residual, and the best weighting of the prediction depends on
the signal-to-noise ratio of the input [@srinivasan1982predictive]. Mumford
proposed that the cortex as a whole is organized like this, with the
feedback from a higher area carrying its reconstruction of the activity in
the lower area and the feedforward path carrying only what remains
unexplained [@mumford1992neocortex], and Rao and Ballard built the
hierarchical network and trained it on natural images [@rao1999predictive].
Their best-known result is the *end-stopping* of visual neurons, i.e., a
unit that responds to a short bar responds progressively less when the bar
is extended beyond its receptive field: the long bar is predicted from its
surroundings, so there is little residual left to report.

Under the FEP this becomes a circuit with two kinds of units at every level
of a hierarchy (@fig-fep-predictive-coding a, b). State units hold the
current estimate of the causes at their level and send a prediction to the
level below; error units at that lower level compare the prediction with
what is actually there and send back the difference, multiplied by a gain.
Three rules govern the traffic: i) predictions descend and errors ascend;
ii) an error that has been explained is silenced, so that at equilibrium
only the unexplained part of the input travels upward, namely the news;
and iii) a state unit moves in the direction that reduces the errors it
receives, from below and from above. The picture to keep is of a hierarchy
in which each level tries to quieten the level below. Perception in this
scheme is not a reconstruction of the scene assembled upward from the
retina but a guess issued downward and corrected by whatever it failed to
predict; what climbs the hierarchy is a report of the misfit, not a copy of
the world. The everyday analogy is proofreading one's own text: a fluent
reader predicts the next word and looks only where the prediction fails,
which is why a typo in a familiar word is so easily missed, and why it is
found when one reads slowly, i.e., when the gain on the sensory error is
turned up. Anatomically, the FEP assigns the errors to the superficial
pyramidal cells that send forward connections and the predictions to the
deep pyramidal cells that send backward connections
[@friston2005theory; @bastos2012canonical]; the general scheme for
hierarchies of dynamical models in continuous time is given in
[@friston2008hierarchical].

![Predictive coding as a picture. (a) The circuit of Example 1: predictions (navy) descend from a state unit to the error unit of the level below, the state of each level enters its own error unit (grey), and the precision-weighted errors (rust) return to the state unit, which follows the negative gradient of the free energy. (b) The same motif stacked into a hierarchy: each level explains the one below, and only the residual, scaled by its precision $\Pi$, ascends. (c) The origin of the name: a channel that transmits the residual between a signal and its prediction carries little until something unpredicted happens. Drawn by `code/fep-predictive-coding.py`.](../figures/fep-predictive-coding.png){#fig-fep-predictive-coding width="100%"}

The rules are not an extra hypothesis; they are the gradient of the free
energy read as a wiring diagram. For Example 1, with a point estimate
$\phi$ in place of $q$, the free energy of @eq-fep-vfe is, up to a
constant, a sum of two squared and precision-weighted errors,
$F(\phi) = (\phi - v_p)^2/(2\Sigma_p) + (u - \phi^2)^2/(2\Sigma_u)$, and
gradient descent on it is exactly Bogacz's network: three nodes, the state
$\phi$ and the prediction errors $\varepsilon_p = (\phi - v_p)/\Sigma_p$ and
$\varepsilon_u = (u - \phi^2)/\Sigma_u$, with the dynamics
$\dot\phi = 2\phi\, \varepsilon_u - \varepsilon_p = -\partial F/\partial\phi$
[@bogacz2017tutorial]. Each error unit needs only the prediction from above
and the signal from below, and the state unit needs only the two errors and
the local slope $2\phi$ of its own prediction. This locality is the point
of the construction: no unit knows the posterior, yet the network finds it.
Numerically $\phi$ converges to $1.5675$ and the error nodes to
$\varepsilon_p = -1.4325$ and $\varepsilon_u = -0.4570$, which are the
analytic values at the mode (@fig-fep-perception c). The network therefore
computes the *mode* of the posterior, not its mean, and the uncertainty has
to be supplied separately by the Laplace approximation
[@friston2007laplace]: the curvature at the mode gives $s = 0.2918$, which
understates both the posterior standard deviation $0.3425$ and the $0.3025$
of the best Gaussian.

The errors are weighted by their *precisions*, i.e., the inverse variances
$1/\Sigma_p$ and $1/\Sigma_u$, and a precision is simply the gain of an
error unit: it decides how loudly a given misfit is reported. Since the
state unit balances the two reports, what matters for the estimate is their
ratio. Specifically, in Example 1 the mode is $1.5675$ at equal precisions;
making the sensory channel four times more precise moves it to $1.4601$,
towards the $\sqrt{u} = 1.4142$ that the data alone would give, and making
the prior four times more precise moves it to $1.8171$, towards the prior
mean $3$, and the same $1.8171$ is obtained by leaving the prior alone and
making the sensory channel four times less precise. The FEP reads attention
as inference about precision [@feldman2010attention]: a cue that a sensory
channel is reliable raises the precision of its errors, and the state units
then follow that channel more closely. In the circuit this is a change of
gain, not a change of wiring, and it is, in effect, the knob that
Srinivasan et al. had already found the retina turning with the
signal-to-noise ratio. Notably,
predictive coding is the process theory for continuous states; the
discrete-state schemes of @sec-fep-core-action minimize the same free energy
with a different message passing [@friston2017process]. For the broader
view of predictive processing in cognitive science, see the review of Clark
and the introduction of Sprevak and Smith
[@clark2013whatever; @sprevak2023introduction].

### Learning and model selection {#sec-fep-core-learning}

Learning uses the same quantity. Under the FEP, parameters are slowly
varying hidden variables, and beliefs about them are updated by minimizing
the free energy averaged over observations. In the standard discrete-state
scheme the likelihood matrix $\mathbf{A}$ and the transition matrices
$\mathbf{B}$ carry Dirichlet priors, and learning accumulates their
concentration parameters after each observation [@friston2016learning; @dacosta2020discrete]; in the limit of point estimates this is EM, with the
E-step minimizing over the hidden states and the M-step over the parameters
[@neal1998em]. In the third line of @eq-fep-vfe the complexity term
penalizes departures from the prior and the accuracy term rewards the fit, so
the free energy is also a computable bound on the negative log model
evidence, which serves for model comparison. Structure learning in active
inference adds hidden-state slots for novel concepts and uses Bayesian model
reduction to reset them in favour of a simpler model with higher evidence
[@smith2020structure].

### Action: active inference and the expected free energy {#sec-fep-core-action}

Action enters the FEP in two ways. i) In continuous-state formulations it
minimizes $F$ directly, by changing the observations so that they conform to
predictions — motor control as the fulfilment of prior expectations about
proprioception [@friston2010action]. ii) In discrete-state formulations the
agent infers policies $\pi$, i.e., sequences of actions, scoring them by the
*expected free energy* [@friston2015epistemic; @friston2017process; @dacosta2020discrete],

$$
\begin{aligned}
G(\pi) \;&=\; \underbrace{\mathrm{KL}\big(q(o \mid \pi) \,\Vert\, \tilde p(o)\big)}_{\text{risk}}
\;+\; \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q(s \mid \pi)}\, H\big[p(o \mid s)\big]}_{\text{ambiguity}} \\
&=\; \underbrace{-\,\mathbb{E}_{q(o \mid \pi)}\big[\log \tilde p(o)\big]}_{-\,\text{pragmatic value}}
\;-\; \underbrace{I_\pi(S; O)}_{\text{epistemic value}} ,
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-fep-efe}

where $q(o \mid \pi) = \mathbb{E}_{q(s \mid \pi)} p(o \mid s)$ is the
predicted distribution of outcomes, $\tilde p(o)$ the *preferences*, termed
prior preferences in the literature, and
$I_\pi(S; O) = H[q(o \mid \pi)] - \mathbb{E}_{q(s \mid \pi)} H[p(o \mid s)]$
the mutual information between hidden states and outcomes, i.e., the expected
information gain. The first line reads "risk plus ambiguity" and the second
"minus pragmatic value minus epistemic value"; exploration and exploitation
thus sit inside one quantity, and Friston et al. note the formal consistency
with the InfoMax principle and with risk-sensitive KL control themselves
[@friston2015epistemic]. The posterior over policies is a softmax,

$$
q(\pi) \;=\; \sigma\big(\log E(\pi) - \gamma\, G(\pi)\big) ,
$$ {#eq-fep-policy}

with $E$ a prior over policies and $\gamma$ a precision. Da Costa et al. call
$\gamma$ an inverse temperature that denotes the confidence in selecting a
policy [@dacosta2020discrete]; in the tutorial of Smith et al. the prior $E$
reflects the number of times a policy has previously been chosen, which
models habits, and $\gamma$ has a prior of its own and is inferred
[@smith2022tutorial]. Experimentally, midbrain activity tracks
trial-by-trial model-based estimates of precision
[@schwartenbeck2015dopamine]. It is worth being careful about what @eq-fep-efe is and is not: it is not simply the free energy of the future
[@millidge2021whence], and several non-equivalent objectives have been
proposed for the same role [@parr2019generalised; @sajid2021demystified; @champion2024reframing]; we return to this in @sec-fep-recent.

**Example 2 (a T-maze with a cue, and the dark room).** A hidden context
$c \in \{L, R\}$ decides whether a reward lies in the left or the right arm,
with prior $(1/2, 1/2)$. The agent may stay at the centre, visit a cue that
reveals the context with validity $v$, enter an arm (reward or loss with
probability $0.98$, after which it cannot leave), or enter a dark room (after
which it cannot leave). The preferences are $\tilde p \propto e^{C}$ with
$C = +3$ for the reward, $-3$ for the loss, and 0 otherwise, so that
$\tilde p$ is $0.8322$ for the reward, $0.0021$ for the loss, and $0.0414$
for each neutral outcome.

| Action | Cross-entropy | $H[q(o)]$ | Ambiguity | Risk | Information gain | $G$ |
|------------------------|------------:|----------:|----------:|----------:|------------:|----------:|
| centre | 3.1837 | 0 | 0 | 3.1837 | 0 | 3.1837 |
| cue, $v = 1$ | 3.1837 | 0.6931 | 0 | 2.4905 | 0.6931 | **2.4905** |
| cue, $v = 0.9$ | 3.1837 | 0.6931 | 0.3251 | 2.4905 | 0.3681 | 2.8156 |
| left (= right) | 3.1837 | 0.6931 | 0.0980 | 2.4905 | 0.5951 | 2.5886 |
| dark | 3.1837 | 0 | 0 | 3.1837 | 0 | 3.1837 |

: One-step expected free energy of each action in Example 2, in nats. Because the preferences are symmetric, the cross-entropy is the same for every action and the first choice is decided by the epistemic term alone; the rows for the centre, the arms, and the dark room do not depend on the cue validity $v$. {#tbl-fep-tmaze}

Three features of @tbl-fep-tmaze are worth noting. First, the symmetry of the
preferences makes the cross-entropy — minus the pragmatic value — equal to
$3.1837$ nats for every action, so the first move is decided by the epistemic
term alone. Second, the two actions with the *lowest* outcome entropy, the
centre and the dark room, have the *highest* expected free energy. This is
the precise form of the answer to the dark-room objection. Critics asked why
an agent that minimizes surprise does not retreat into a dark and unchanging
room; Friston, Thornton, and Clark replied that average surprise is a
function of the sensations *and of the agent predicting them*, whereas the
entropy that a dark room minimizes is a function of the sensations alone
[@friston2012darkroom], and Schwartenbeck et al. added that minimizing
surprise leads naturally to exploration and to novelty bonuses
[@schwartenbeck2013exploration]. In @tbl-fep-tmaze the reply becomes an
identity: the risk term
$\mathrm{KL}(q(o \mid \pi) \Vert \tilde p) = \mathrm{CE} - H[q(o \mid \pi)]$
subtracts the outcome entropy from the expected surprise, so an agent
minimizing @eq-fep-efe does not minimize the entropy of its outcomes, and the
dark room is chosen only if the preferences themselves favour it. Third, the
epistemic term is sensitive to reliability: with a perfect cue the
information gain is $\log 2 = 0.6931$ against $0.5951$ for an arm, so the
agent looks at the cue; at a validity of $0.9$ the ambiguity rises to
$0.3251$ and the one-step choice flips to entering an arm. The precision
$\gamma$ sets how deterministic the choice is: with a reliable cue, the
probability of visiting the cue under @eq-fep-policy with a flat $E$ is only
$0.262$ at $\gamma = 1$, $0.404$ at $\gamma = 4$, and $0.706$ at
$\gamma = 16$ (@fig-fep-tmaze b).

![Planning with the expected free energy (Example 2). (a) Cross-entropy to the preferences, minus the information gain, and $G$ for each action with a fully reliable cue; (b) the precision dial $q(a) \propto e^{-\gamma G(a)}$; (c) one-step $G$ (dots) against the sophisticated two-step value (bars) at two cue validities. Produced by `code/fep-examples.py`.](../figures/fep-tmaze.png){#fig-fep-tmaze width="100%"}

That last flip is an artefact of myopia, and it is worth saying so, because
the one-step expected free energy is often presented as the whole story.
*Sophisticated inference* computes $G$ recursively: the expected free energy
of the next action is its own risk and ambiguity plus the average expected
free energy of the beliefs that would follow under counterfactual outcomes
and subsequent actions, the latter weighted by a softmax of their own $G$, so
that it is a tree search over beliefs about beliefs
[@friston2021sophisticated]. In the high-precision limit the two-step value
is $G(a_1) + \mathbb{E}_{o_1} \min_{a_2} G(a_2 \mid o_1)$. Under that score,
visiting the cue first is best at both validities — $2.7942$ at $v = 1$ and
$3.4344$ at $v = 0.9$, against $5.6742$ for staying at the centre, $5.7049$
for entering an arm, and $6.3674$ for the dark room — which corrects the
one-step choice (@fig-fep-tmaze c). By contrast, a score that adds two
one-step values of $G$ under the same prior belief selects "cue, then cue
again" ($4.9811$) at $v = 1$ and "left, then left" ($5.1771$) at $v = 0.9$,
because it does not let the second step use the first observation. This
matches the result of Da Costa et al.: the standard scheme is Bellman optimal
for a planning horizon of one and not beyond, whereas sophisticated inference
is Bellman optimal on any finite horizon [@dacosta2023reward].

### Markov blankets, steady states, and Bayesian mechanics {#sec-fep-blankets}

The most ambitious part of the FEP is not an algorithm but a physical claim
about existence. In "Life as we know it", Friston argues that if a set of
dynamical systems is coupled only by short-range forces, then remote states
are conditionally independent, which induces a *Markov blanket* separating
internal from external states; the internal states then appear to minimize
a free-energy functional of the blanket states, i.e., appear to infer the
external world. He goes on to argue that, since the long-term average of
surprise is an entropy, minimizing free energy by selectively sampling the
world places an upper bound on the entropy of the sensory states, which in
his words enables biological systems to resist the second law of
thermodynamics [@friston2013life]. Kirchhoff et al. nest the construction
into blankets of blankets [@kirchhoff2018blankets], and Ramstead et al.
extend it to the capacity of living systems to avoid decay, in answer to
Schrödinger's question [@ramstead2018schrodinger].

After 2019 this part developed into *Bayesian mechanics*. Starting from a
Langevin equation, sparse coupling yields a *particular partition*, and the
paths of the internal states of a particle obey a principle of least action
which, read teleologically, maximizes the marginal likelihood
[@friston2019particular; @friston2023simpler]; "strange" particles also
infer their own actions [@friston2023path]. Da Costa et al. give a more
careful treatment for stationary processes, in which the internal states
appear to perform variational inference and the active states can be read as
performing active inference, covering classical stochastic control such as
PID control [@dacosta2021stationary]. Ramstead et al. distinguish
path-tracking, mode-tracking, and mode-matching mechanics and examine a
duality between the FEP and the constrained maximum entropy principle
[@ramstead2023bayesian]; Sakthivadivel argues that for a class of constrained
dynamics the inference is equivalent to gradient ascent on a Shannon entropy
functional [@sakthivadivel2022geometry]; a quantum-information version is due
to Fields et al. [@fields2022quantum].

This is also where the controversy concentrates, and the critiques are taken
up in @sec-fep-critiques. Two points matter for what follows. The
mathematics of @sec-fep-vfe to @sec-fep-core-action does not depend on the
physical assumptions about blankets and steady states; and, conversely, the
physical claims do not follow from the entropy-based learning of this book,
as we explain in @sec-fep-duality.

### A map of the principle {#sec-fep-map}

The FEP therefore operates at several levels at once, and much of the
confusion around it comes from not saying which level is meant. @tbl-fep-map lists the levels, the object and the quantity minimized at
each, and the counterpart in this book, which @sec-fep-connections
establishes row by row.

| Level | Object in the FEP | Quantity minimized | Counterpart in this book |
|---------------|------------------|----------------------|--------------------------------------|
| perception | belief $q(s)$ | $F[q; o]$, @eq-fep-vfe | @eq-max-def-free at $T = 1$ with $h = p(s)$; @sec-fep-one |
| predictive coding | mode $\phi$, precisions | $-\log p(o, \phi)$, plus curvature | the $T \to 0$ end of the dial with a Laplace correction; @sec-fep-perception |
| learning | parameters $\theta$ | average $F$ | maximum-entropy learning with missing data (@sec-max-boundary); $T = 1$ on the dial of @sec-minimax-label-temperature; @sec-fep-learning |
| model selection | model $m$ | $F$ as a bound on $-\log p(o \mid m)$ | Type I with a cost on the parameters; MDL (@sec-minimax-principle); @sec-fep-modelsel |
| planning | policy $\pi$ | $G(\pi)$, @eq-fep-efe | firmness plus fairness (@sec-min-history); Type III, proposed in @sec-fep-typeIII |
| policy selection | $q(\pi)$, @eq-fep-policy | $\mathbb{E}_q[G] + \gamma^{-1} \mathrm{KL}(q \Vert E)$ | the Gibbs tilts @eq-min-gibbs and @eq-post-tilt; @sec-fep-tilt |
| existence | steady-state density, blankets | average surprise | not derivable; a duality with maximum entropy; @sec-fep-duality |

: The levels of the free-energy principle and their counterparts in this book. {#tbl-fep-map}

## Recent developments, 2019–2026 {#sec-fep-recent}

### Critiques and replies {#sec-fep-critiques}

The principle has been examined closely since 2020, and the examination has
drawn detailed replies; in our reading the exchange is still open. We group
the main lines under three headings, state each position as its authors
state it, and do not attempt to settle the matter. Two cautions apply
throughout. First, much of the technical discussion concerns the 2013
formulation of @sec-fep-blankets, and the critics themselves note that the
later formulations parametrize the variational density by different
variables and carry a different interpretation [@biehl2021critique], so
that an objection to one formulation is not automatically an objection to
another. Second, the variational free energy of @sec-fep-vfe and its use in
perception and learning, which is most of what this chapter draws on, is
not what is in dispute; the disputes concern the physical claims about
blankets and steady states, the objective for planning, and the epistemic
status of the principle as a whole.

i\) *Technical.* Biehl, Pollock, and Kanai examine the formulation of "Life
as we know it" and report that the definitions of the Markov blanket used in
different papers are not equivalent, that the steps which rewrite the
equations of motion of a system with a blanket are not generally correct
without additional assumptions that had not been stated, and that the
free-energy lemma, taken at face value, admits counterexamples; where the
lemma does hold, they show, the variational density coincides with the
conditional density of the steady state, and since the interpretation in
terms of Bayesian inference hinges on this point they conclude that it is
not sufficiently justified. They add that the problems they raise do not
rule out that the general ideas behind the principle are worth pursuing
[@biehl2021critique]. Friston, Da Costa, and Parr take the observations as
bearing on an early formulation and use them to set out the technical
arguments that underwrite the principle, with the discussion focusing on
solenoidal coupling between subsets of states in sparsely coupled systems
and on the distinction between exact and approximate Bayesian inference
[@friston2021observations]. Aguilera et al. examine the simplest setting,
weakly coupled linear stochastic systems, and report that the blanket
condition and the restrictions on solenoidal flow are met only in a narrow
region of parameter space, requiring an absence of perception–action
asymmetry that they consider unusual for living systems, and that the step
from the dynamics to variational inference relies on an equivalence between
the dynamics of the average states and the average of the dynamics which
does not hold in general even for linear systems; they conclude that more
development is needed before the theory can be applied to living and
cognitive systems [@aguilera2022particular]. Friston replied in a comment
[@friston2022veryparticular], and Heins and Da Costa worked out, for
Gaussian steady states and for linear and nonlinear dynamics alike, the
conditions under which sparse coupling does or does not give rise to a
Markov blanket [@heins2022sparse]; the authors' response moves the
discussion toward what they term a confederation of Bayesian mechanics
[@aguilera2023confederation]. The later formulations surveyed in @sec-fep-blankets state their starting point as a partition defined by
conditional independences that inherit from sparsely coupled dynamics
[@friston2023simpler; @dacosta2021stationary; @ramstead2023bayesian]; how
far this meets the objections is, in our reading, still being worked out on
both sides.

ii\) *Conceptual.* Bruineberg et al. trace the Markov blanket from its use
in Bayesian networks to its use in active inference, distinguish *Pearl
blankets*, an epistemic tool for Bayesian inference, from *Friston
blankets*, a construct meant to demarcate the physical boundary between an
agent and its environment, and argue that the literature has not kept the
two apart; only the second, they hold, can do metaphysical work, and it
requires philosophical premises that the success of the mathematics does
not by itself supply [@bruineberg2022emperor]. The paper appeared as a
target article with thirty-five commentaries, which take many different
stances, and the authors' reply [@bruineberg2022naked]. Raja et al. argue
that the FEP generalizes Bayesian inference to all domains by way of the
blanket formalism, which they term the Markov blanket trick, and that active
inference presupposes successful perception and action instead of explaining
them [@raja2021blanket]; Friston replied in a comment, and the authors
responded [@friston2022ultimate; @raja2023trick]. Colombo and Wright note
that the FEP has been called a postulate, an unfalsifiable principle, a
natural law, and an imperative, that its epistemic status is unclear, and
that it might nevertheless afford a theoretical foundation for the relation
between environment, life, and mind; they set out limits and prospects for
it as a first principle in the life sciences [@colombo2021first]. Andrews
takes both the positive and the negative evaluations to date to have been
largely in error: the FEP, on his account, is a model structure, i.e., a
modelling language to which construals are added to make FEP models, so
that demands that the principle itself be falsifiable or biologically
realistic rest on a category error — the mathematics is not the territory
[@andrews2021math].

iii\) *On the expected free energy.* Millidge, Tschantz, and Buckley
investigate where the expected free energy comes from and argue that it is
not simply the free energy in the future: a functional that they take to be
the natural extension of @eq-fep-vfe into the future actively discourages
exploration, so that exploration does not directly follow from minimizing
free energy ahead of time, and they develop the free energy of the expected
future as an alternative objective [@millidge2021whence]. Gottwald and
Braun distinguish two notions of free energy in current models of
intelligent agency, both of them applications of Bayesian inference to
action selection, namely one that appears when trading off accuracy against
uncertainty under a general maximum-entropy principle, and one that
formulates action selection as minimizing the deviation of beliefs and
policies from reference models, which is active inference
[@gottwald2020two]. The free energy of this book is of the first kind, as
we make precise in @sec-fep-one; the subsequent theory of the expected free
energy, which addresses part of the question raised by Millidge et al., is
the subject of @sec-fep-planning.

### Planning and the theory of the expected free energy {#sec-fep-planning}

The status of the expected free energy has nevertheless been clarified
considerably. Parr and Friston compare two functionals: in the expected free
energy, prior beliefs about outcomes are not part of the generative model
but are absorbed into the prior over policies, whereas in the *generalized*
free energy they become an explicit part of the model
[@parr2019generalised]. Da Costa et al. give a complete synthesis of active
inference on discrete state spaces [@dacosta2020discrete], and sophisticated
inference and its Bellman optimality were discussed in @sec-fep-core-action
[@friston2021sophisticated; @dacosta2023reward]. Sajid et al. compare active
inference with reinforcement learning on the same environments and stress
that reward can be treated as one more observation over which the agent has
a preference [@sajid2021demystified]. Champion et al. formalize the
*unification problem* — deriving the various forms of the expected free
energy from a single root definition — and find that in one setting all the
forms are recovered, but that the root definition itself has no justification
to date and admits only a limited class of preferences
[@champion2024reframing]. Most recently, de Vries et al. and Nuijten et al.
show that planning with the expected free energy can be written as
variational free-energy minimization on a generative model augmented with
*epistemic priors* [@devries2025efe; @nuijten2026efe]; Nuijten et al. then
rewrite the free energy of the augmented model as that of the predictive
model plus explicit entropy corrections, and note that full planning also
needs a correction that turns marginal inference into policy optimization
[@nuijten2026type]. Sweeney et al. develop the formal correspondences between
expected-free-energy minimization and Bayesian decision theory, resource
rationality, optimal control, reinforcement learning, rate–distortion theory,
and maximum entropy [@sweeney2026decision].

### Deep and scalable active inference {#sec-fep-deep}

Taking active inference from small discrete problems to high-dimensional
tasks has been the main engineering direction. Ueltzhöffer combines it with
variational inference in deep generative models and with evolution
strategies, and obtains goal-directed behaviour on the mountain-car problem
[@ueltzhoffer2018deep]; Millidge approximates the key densities by deep
networks, obtains performance comparable with common reinforcement-learning
baselines on OpenAI Gym benchmarks, and notes the similarities with
maximum-entropy reinforcement learning and with policy gradients
[@millidge2020dpg]; Tschantz et al. take the free energy of the expected
future as the objective and balance exploration and exploitation on
benchmarks with sparse, well-shaped, and no rewards [@tschantz2020rl]; and
Fountas et al. build deep agents with Monte Carlo tree search, a habitual
network, and MC dropout [@fountas2020deep]. Surveys are those of Mazzaglia et
al., from the side of deep learning [@mazzaglia2022deep], and of Lanillos et
al., for robotics [@lanillos2021robotics]; software includes pymdp
[@heins2022pymdp] and RxInfer [@bagaev2023rxinfer]. The latest step is the
*renormalizing generative model*, which generalizes partially observed
Markov decision processes to include paths as latent variables and uses the
renormalization group to build deep, scale-invariant models, applied to
image classification, to the compression and generation of movies and music,
and to Atari-like games [@friston2025pixels]; AXIOM uses object-centric core
priors to accelerate the learning of games in the low-data regime
[@heins2025axiom]. Closest to machine learning, Hafner et al. introduce the
*action–perception divergence*, a single principle that covers
representation learning, information gain, empowerment, and skill discovery,
with agents that use perception to align their beliefs with the world and
action to align the world with their beliefs [@hafner2020divergence].

### Experimental tests {#sec-fep-empirical}

The evidence concentrates on in vitro neural networks and on human
decision-making. Isomura and Friston stimulated in vitro cortical cultures
with stimulus trains of known statistical structure and found the recorded
responses consistent with variational message passing [@isomura2018invitro];
Isomura et al. show that a class of canonical neural networks with delayed
modulation of Hebbian plasticity implicitly performs active inference
[@isomura2022canonical]; and in 2023 Isomura et al. used in vitro networks of
rat cortical neurons that separate two mixed hidden sources to confirm
quantitative predictions — pharmacological up- and down-regulation of
excitability disrupted the inference in the way that a change of prior
would, and changes in effective synaptic connectivity reduced the variational
free energy [@isomura2023experimental]. The DishBrain of Kagan et al.
embedded in vitro neurons in a simulated game of Pong and reports learning
within minutes [@kagan2022invitro]; its use of the word "sentience" drew a
public response [@balci2023response]. In humans, Schwartenbeck et al. found
with fMRI that midbrain activity tracks model-based estimates of precision
[@schwartenbeck2015dopamine]. These results test particular process theories
rather than the principle as such, and Isomura et al. say so explicitly:
empirical applications entail a commitment to a particular process theory
[@isomura2023experimental].

### Generative AI and agents {#sec-fep-ai}

Since 2023 the FEP literature has addressed generative AI directly. Pezzulo
et al. argue that the generative models of living organisms are anchored to
the body and the world: unlike the passive models learned by generative AI,
they must capture and control the sensory consequences of action, which in
their view is what understanding rests on [@pezzulo2024generating]. Friston
et al. read intelligence as the capacity to accumulate evidence for a
generative model of one's sensed world, i.e., self-evidencing in the sense of
Hohwy [@hohwy2016selfevidencing], and envisage an ecosystem of shared
intelligence built on active inference [@friston2024ecosystems]. On the
engineering side, Dutta et al. cast context acquisition by interactive AI
agents — clarifying questions, retrieval, tool calls — as active inference:
an inner step updates beliefs over a latent task state, and an outer decision
selects the next action to minimize the expected free energy under a cost; in
deterministic settings the epistemic term reduces to the expected
information gain, and they benchmark frontier language models on an
optimal-question-asking task [@dutta2026context]. We return to this
structure, inference inside and the choice of data outside, in @sec-fep-ceiling.
