## Connections to entropy-based learning {#sec-fep-connections}


This concludes our review of the principle in its own language. Now, let us
reinterpret it in the framework developed throughout this book, moving step
by step along the levels summarized in @tbl-fep-map. The point to hold on
to, at the outset, is that the central translations below are identities,
not analogies; where a translation is only a correspondence, or a reading
of ours, @tbl-fep-corr says so.

### One free energy {#sec-fep-one}

The first line of @eq-fep-vfe is the free energy of @sec-max-def-representation with a particular assignment of base measure and
energy.

::: {.callout-note title="Proposition 1 (one free energy)"}
For a generative model $p(o, s) = p(s)\, p(o \mid s)$, the variational free
energy @eq-fep-vfe equals $\mathcal{F}_T(q; E)$ of @eq-max-def-free with
$h = p(s)$, $E(s) = -\log p(o \mid s)$, and $T = 1$. It also equals
$\mathcal{F}_1$ with a flat base measure and the energy
$E(s) = -\log p(o, s)$. In both readings the minimizer is the posterior
$p(s \mid o)$ and the minimum is $-\log Z = -\log p(o)$. For a general
temperature the two readings differ: the minimizers are
$q_T \propto p(s)\, p(o \mid s)^{1/T}$ and $q_T \propto p(o, s)^{1/T}$,
respectively.
:::

The proof is a substitution: $\mathbb{E}_q[-\log p(o \mid s)] +
\mathrm{KL}(q \Vert p(s))$ is the third line of @eq-fep-vfe, and
$Z = \int p(s)\, p(o \mid s)\, ds = p(o)$. Two remarks are worth making.
First, in perception under the FEP, $T = 1$ is not a dial that someone
chooses; it is the point at which Bayes' rule itself sits. Writing Bayes'
rule as a variational problem is an old result in statistics, which goes
back to the Donsker–Varadhan formula, to Williams' principle of minimum
information, and to Zellner's optimal information processing
[@donsker1975asymptotic; @williams1980bayesian; @zellner1988optimal]; Giffin
and Caticha process data and moment constraints simultaneously by maximum
relative entropy [@giffin2007updating], which is the constrained and the
free-energy form of @sec-max-def-representation unified in Bayesian
updating. Second, replacing the negative log-likelihood by a general loss, or
the KL divergence by another divergence, gives general Bayesian updating and
generalized variational inference [@bissiri2016general; @knoblauch2022gvi],
i.e., the generalized sense of @sec-max-boundary.

Notably, the two readings of Proposition 1 are not a technicality. They are
the two ways of splitting a model into a base measure and an energy, and the
rest of this section shows that the FEP uses both, at different levels, and
that several of its apparent puzzles dissolve once one asks which split is in
force. Proposition 1 also concerns the variational free energy only, and it
is worth placing it in the distinction of Gottwald and Braun (@sec-fep-critiques). Their first kind, the *free energy from constraints*,
is an energy traded against an entropy with a multiplier that is determined
by a constraint, which is @eq-max-def-free; their second kind, the
*variational free energy*, is an error measure between a trial distribution
$q$ and an unnormalized reference function $\phi$, namely
$\mathbb{E}_q[-\log \phi] - H(q)$, introduced as a device for representing a
normalization as an optimization problem, which is the first line of @eq-fep-vfe with $\phi = p(o, s)$. They note that the two expressions are
transformed into each other by $\phi = h\, e^{-E/T}$, and insist that they
nevertheless differ in method and motivation: the first presupposes a
constrained quantity and a trade-off, the second presupposes neither
[@gottwald2020two]. Proposition 1 is that transformation at $T = 1$, and its
second reading is exactly their second kind. The free energy of this book is
of the first kind; the expected free energy @eq-fep-efe is a further object
of the second kind, built for action selection, which is not the same object
as @eq-fep-vfe, and we come to it in @sec-fep-typeIII.

### Perception: two readings of the dial {#sec-fep-perception}

Example 1 showed that predictive coding computes the mode of the posterior
and not its mean, with the uncertainty supplied afterwards by the Laplace
approximation. This is the first place where the distinction of Proposition
1 earns its keep. Predictive coding is the $T \to 0$ end of the *second*
reading, in which the energy is $-\log p(o, s)$ and lowering the temperature
concentrates the belief on the maximum a posteriori value without moving it.

**Precision is a temperature.** For a Gaussian likelihood, lowering the
temperature of the likelihood term from 1 to $T$ is the same as raising the
sensory precision from $1/\Sigma_u$ to $1/(T\Sigma_u)$, since
$p(u \mid v)^{1/T} \propto \mathcal{N}(u; v^2, T\Sigma_u)$. This is the
*first* reading of Proposition 1, in which the prior is the base measure and
the dial of @sec-free-energy acts on the likelihood alone. In Example 1 the
mode of $q_T \propto p(v)\, p(u \mid v)^{1/T}$ moves from $1.817$ at $T = 4$,
towards the prior mean $3$, through $1.5675$ at $T = 1$, to $1.418$ at
$T = 0.02$, approaching the maximum-likelihood value $\sqrt{2} = 1.4142$;
under the second reading the mode stays at $1.5675$ for every $T$, while the
mean moves from $1.480$ at $T = 1$ to $1.566$ at $T = 0.02$, towards the
mode. Attention as inference about precision (@sec-fep-pc) is,
in our terms, inference about a likelihood temperature. Perception itself
stays at $T = 1$.

In the classification of @sec-max-definition, perception has only the levels
i) and ii), representation and inference, with no learner: it is inference
over a maximum-entropy model, and nothing is fitted.

### Learning: minimax entropy at $T = 1$ {#sec-fep-learning}

We saw in @sec-fep-core-learning that learning under the FEP minimizes the
same free energy, and that in the limit of point estimates it is EM. The
question for this book is which outer problem that is. The answer is sharper
than we expected.

::: {.callout-note title="Proposition 2 (learning as a difference of entropies)"}
Let the complete-data model
$p_\theta(o, s) \propto h(o, s) \exp\big(\boldsymbol{\lambda}^{\top}
\mathsf{T}(o, s)\big)$ be an exponential family in the sufficient statistics
$\mathsf{T}$ with a uniform base measure $h$. Given data $o_1, \dots, o_n$
and any conditional distribution $q(s \mid o)$, let $\boldsymbol{\lambda}$ be
the M-step fit to the completed data $\hat p(o)\, q(s \mid o)$, i.e.,
$\mathbb{E}_{\hat p q}[\mathsf{T}] = \mathbb{E}_{p_\theta}[\mathsf{T}]$. Then
for every label temperature $T \ge 0$,

$$
\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \Big\{ \mathbb{E}_{q(\cdot \mid o_i)}\big[-\log p_\theta(o_i, s)\big] - T\, H\big(q(\cdot \mid o_i)\big) \Big\}
\;=\; H\big(p_\theta(O, S)\big) - T\, \overline{H(q)} ,
$$ {#eq-fep-learning}

where $\overline{H(q)} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_i H\big(q(\cdot \mid o_i)\big)$. At
$T = 1$ the left-hand side is the average variational free energy @eq-fep-vfe.
:::

The proof is that of @eq-max-bridge. For a uniform $h$ we have
$-\log p_\theta(o, s) = -\boldsymbol{\lambda}^{\top} \mathsf{T}(o, s) +
\log Z(\boldsymbol{\lambda})$ up to a constant, so the cross-entropy on the
completed data equals $-\boldsymbol{\lambda}^{\top}
\mathbb{E}_{\hat p q}[\mathsf{T}] + \log Z =
-\boldsymbol{\lambda}^{\top} \mathbb{E}_{p_\theta}[\mathsf{T}] + \log Z =
H(p_\theta)$; subtracting $T\, \overline{H(q)}$ gives @eq-fep-learning. If
the statistics also depend on representation parameters $\theta'$, writing
$p^\star_{\theta', q}$ for the maximum-entropy model of the completed data
and $\ell_T$ for the label free energy @eq-mm-label-free gives

$$
\min_{\theta}\; \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n} \ell_T(\theta; o_i)
\;=\; \min_{\theta',\, q} \Big\{ H\big(p^\star_{\theta', q}\big) - T\, \overline{H(q)} \Big\} ,
$$ {#eq-fep-learning-minimax}

whose $T \to 0$ end is @eq-mm-minimax-labels, the classification likelihood,
and whose $T = 1$ end is the marginal likelihood, i.e., EM.

Proposition 2 is a direct consequence of @eq-max-bridge, and @eq-mm-plugin,
the decomposition of Hathaway [@hathaway1986em], is its counterpart on the
side of the E-step; we claim no priority for either. What we want the reader
to take from it is the *reading*. The average free energy is the entropy of
the world model minus the entropy of the inferred causes. Learning under the
FEP is therefore minimax-entropy learning whose outer problem minimizes the
entropy of the world model — which is Type I of @sec-minimax-two-questions —
while the inner problem keeps the entropy of the causes at full weight. The
interpolation between the two ends that @sec-minimax-label-temperature
describes is exactly the $T$ of @eq-fep-learning, and the FEP sits at one
particular setting of it.

**Example 3 (learning).** We draw $n = 2000$ samples from
$0.4\, \mathcal{N}(-1, 0.7^2) + 0.6\, \mathcal{N}(1, 1)$ and run EM at a
label temperature $T$, with the E-step
$q(s \mid o) \propto p_\theta(o, s)^{1/T}$ — a hard assignment at $T = 0$ —
and the M-step matching the moments of the completed data. At every
temperature and every iteration the two sides of @eq-fep-learning agree to
within $3.8 \times 10^{-15}$, and the objective is non-increasing to within
rounding (@fig-fep-learning a). At $T = 1$, EM converges to
$\hat\pi = (0.399, 0.601)$, $\hat\mu = (-1.034, 1.010)$, and
$\hat\sigma = (0.703, 0.991)$; the average free energy $1.6791$ equals the
training negative log-likelihood to within $10^{-12}$, and it splits into a
world-model entropy of $1.9457$ minus a cause entropy of $0.2666$. On
200,000 held-out samples the negative log-likelihood is $0.4$ millinats above
that of the true distribution. At $T = 0$, which is classification EM
[@celeux1992cem], the entropy of the world model falls to $1.7782$ and that
of the causes to zero, but the means are pushed apart and the variances
shrink, $\hat\mu = (-0.963, 1.291)$ and $\hat\sigma = (0.657, 0.777)$, and
the held-out negative log-likelihood is $17.0$ millinats above the truth,
against $12.3$ at $T = 0.5$ (@fig-fep-learning b, c).

![Learning as free-energy minimization (Example 3). (a) EM at $T = 1$: the entropy of the world model, the entropy of the inferred causes, and their difference, with the average free energy computed directly shown as dots; (b) the label-temperature dial, with the two entropies at convergence on the left axis and the excess of the held-out negative log-likelihood over the truth on the right, in millinats; (c) fitted densities at $T = 1$, $0.5$, and $0$ against the truth. Produced by `code/fep-examples.py`.](../figures/fep-learning.png){#fig-fep-learning width="100%"}

This is what @sec-minimax-label-temperature predicts: a label temperature
below one makes the label side commit, which is Type II, and it pays for the
commitment in the fit of the density to the inputs. Learning under the FEP
declines to make that trade.

One detail deserves mention, since it looks like a contradiction and is not.
We said in @sec-max-boundary that directed graphical models fitted by maximum
likelihood or EM are maximum-entropy learners without being maximum-entropy
models, which is true of the marginal $p_\theta(o)$. Proposition 2 says that
at the level of the *completed* data, EM for an exponential-family mixture is
a minimax-entropy learner. The two statements concern different sets of
variables.

### Model selection: Type I and description length {#sec-fep-modelsel}

Model selection is the same story one level up. Recall that @sec-minimax-principle starts from minimum description length: for a
maximum-entropy model the description length equals the model's own entropy,
$L(P_F) = S(P_F)$, so choosing features for the shortest description is
Type I [@grunwald2007mdl; @feder1986maximum; @carcamo2025minimax]. Model
selection under the FEP uses the free energy as a bound on the negative log
model evidence (@sec-fep-core-learning), and its complexity term for the
parameters, $\mathrm{KL}(q(\theta) \Vert p(\theta))$, is their description
length. This reading is not new to the FEP: Hinton and van Camp read
variational learning as minimizing the description length of the weights
[@hinton1993keeping], Hinton and Zemel read the cost of an autoencoder in
terms of MDL and the Helmholtz free energy [@hinton1994autoencoders], and
Honkela and Valpola explain variational Bayesian learning through bits-back
coding [@honkela2004bitsback].

In the language of this book, then, model selection under the FEP is Type I
with a cost on the parameters: the budget of @sec-minimax-principle is a
number of features, whereas that of the FEP is counted in nats. The outer
criteria differ slightly, in a way worth keeping straight. Type I minimizes
$S(P_F)$, the cross-entropy at the maximum-likelihood fit; the FEP minimizes
a free energy that also carries the uncertainty about the parameters. When
the parameter posterior is concentrated, the free energy of $n$ data points
is approximately $n\, S(P_F)$ plus the cost of the parameters, and the two
agree to leading order. The structure learning of @sec-fep-core-learning,
which adds hidden-state slots and reduces them by Bayesian model reduction,
is the combinatorial search of @sec-minimax-principle conducted in nats.
Notably, the minimax entropy principle has recently yielded exactly solvable
models of large neuronal populations [@lynn2024exact], a natural meeting
point with the neuroscience from which the FEP arose.

### Action: Type III, firm but fair {#sec-fep-typeIII}

The first line of @eq-fep-efe is an object this book has already met, with
the direction of one arrow reversed.

::: {.callout-note title="Proposition 3 (the expected free energy is firm but fair)"}
Write $\bar p_\pi = q(o \mid \pi)$ for the predicted marginal of the
outcomes. Then

$$
G(\pi) \;=\; \underbrace{\mathrm{KL}\big(\bar p_\pi \,\Vert\, \tilde p\big)}_{\text{fairness, target } \tilde p}
\;+\; \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{q(s \mid \pi)} H\big[p(o \mid s)\big]}_{\text{firmness}} ,
$$ {#eq-fep-firmfair}

i.e., the fairness and firmness terms of @sec-min-history, with the hidden
state $s$ in the place of the input, the outcome $o$ in the place of the
label, and the likelihood $p(o \mid s)$ in the place of the classifier. With
flat preferences, $G(\pi) = \log|\mathcal{O}| - I_\pi(S; O)$, so that
minimizing $G$ maximizes the mutual information of Bridle et al.
[@bridle1992phantom]. Unlike in Bridle's case, the variable being optimized
is not the classifier but the distribution $q(s \mid \pi)$ of the inputs, or
the channel $p(o \mid s, \pi)$.
:::

The decomposition into risk and ambiguity is standard [@friston2015epistemic; @dacosta2020discrete]; what we add is the correspondence, which shows that
both entropy terms of the expected free energy have been in this book all
along. The classifier of @sec-min-history is optimized for a fixed
distribution of data; active inference fixes the likelihood and optimizes
*what to look at*. That direction is the one of channel capacity and of
Bayesian experimental design: Lindley measures the information an experiment
provides by the expected information between parameter and data
[@lindley1956measure], MacKay uses it for active data selection
[@mackay1992information], and Linsker's InfoMax maximizes the mutual
information between the input and the output of a perceptual network
[@linsker1988self]. Within the book, @sec-minimax-entropy already observes
that Sustek et al., by adding $I_\theta(X; Y)$ to the objective of a joint
energy-based model, place the mutual-information objective of @sec-min-history on top of a maximum-entropy learner [@sustek2023stabilized];
the expected free energy places the same objective on top of a generative
model and changes the optimized variable from the classifier to the action.

This is the gap in @sec-minimax-two-questions, and we propose to fill it.

::: {.callout-tip title="Definition: minimax-entropy learning of Type III"}
In addition to Types I and II of @sec-minimax-two-questions, we term a method
of **Type III** (*what to observe*) if its outer problem chooses an action, a
policy, or an experiment $\xi$ that decides the data to which the inner model
will be fitted, so as to minimize the expected entropy of the inner model's
posterior over its hidden variables,

$$
\min_{\xi}\; \mathbb{E}_{o \sim q(o \mid \xi)}\, H\big(q(S \mid o, \xi)\big) ,
$$ {#eq-fep-typeIII}

which, when the prior over the hidden variables does not depend on $\xi$, is
the same as maximizing $I_\xi(S; O)$. The outer problem may add a prescribed
marginal of the outcomes, the preferences, as the target of fairness. The
posterior is computed at $T = 1$: the entropy is lowered by the choice of the
data and not by sharpening the posterior. The anchor iii) is then met
*through the world* — the outer entropy is an expectation under the inner
model's own predictive distribution, and the inner model is afterwards fitted
to the data that the chosen action actually produces.
:::

| Type | Outer variable | Entropy minimized | Temperature | Examples |
|---------------|-----------------|----------------------|----------------|--------------------------------|
| I, what to measure | features, model, parameters | entropy of the maximum-entropy model, $S(P_F)$ | inner at $T = 1$ | FRAME; energy-based models by maximum likelihood; EM (Proposition 2); model selection under the FEP |
| II, what to commit to | assignments, classifier | predictive entropy of $Y$ | label at $T < 1$ | softmax classification; classification EM; joint energy-based models with entropy minimization |
| III, what to observe | action, policy, experiment | expected posterior entropy $\mathbb{E}_o H(S \mid o)$ | posterior at $T = 1$; policies at $1/\gamma$ | epistemic value of @eq-fep-efe; Bayesian experimental design; context acquisition by agents |

: The three kinds of outer problem in minimax-entropy learning. Types I and II are those of @sec-minimax-two-questions; Type III is proposed here, and it is the one in which the data are not given. {#tbl-fep-types}

Example 2 shows the type at work and separates it from Type II. The symmetry
of the preferences made the first move a pure Type III decision, settled by
the epistemic term alone. The agent's belief about the context is a Bayesian
posterior at $T = 1$ throughout; it never commits by sharpening that
posterior. It obtains certainty by *fetching the data* on which the
posterior can be confident. Type II lowers the entropy of a belief on fixed
data; Type III goes out and changes the data.

### Policies: Gibbs tilts, and precision as a temperature {#sec-fep-tilt}

The posterior over policies, @eq-fep-policy, is an object from @sec-post-training.

::: {.callout-note title="Proposition 4 (the posterior over policies is a Gibbs tilt)"}
$q(\pi) = \sigma\big(\log E(\pi) - \gamma G(\pi)\big)$ is the unique
minimizer of $\mathbb{E}_q[G] + \gamma^{-1} \mathrm{KL}(q \Vert E)$, with
minimum $-\gamma^{-1} \log \sum_\pi E(\pi)\, e^{-\gamma G(\pi)}$. It is
therefore @eq-max-def-free on the space of policies, with the energy $G$, the
base measure $E$, and the temperature $T = 1/\gamma$; equivalently it is @eq-min-gibbs with reward $-G$ and reference policy $E$, and @eq-post-tilt
with the habits as reference.
:::

Three comparisons follow, and each sharpens something stated loosely
elsewhere. i) *Risk is maximum-entropy control on outcomes.* Since
$\mathrm{KL}(\bar p_\pi \Vert \tilde p) = -H(\bar p_\pi) -
\mathbb{E}_{\bar p_\pi}[C] + \log Z_C$ for $\tilde p \propto e^{C}$,
minimizing the risk maximizes expected utility *plus the entropy of the
outcomes*. The structure is that of @eq-max-rl-objective, but with the
entropy bonus on the outcomes rather than on the actions; Millidge et al.
likewise locate the difference between active inference and control as
inference in how value enters the respective generative models
[@millidge2020cai; @levine2018rlinference]. ii) *Precision is an inferred
temperature.* We called the temperature of @eq-post-tilt a genuine dial,
chosen by the designer (@sec-post-tilt). Active inference gives $\gamma$ a
prior and infers it, and the inferred value has a neural correlate (@sec-fep-core-action). The temperature of a learned energy is not
identifiable when the family is closed under rescaling (@sec-max-def-family); $\gamma$ escapes this because $G$ is measured in nats,
on a fixed scale. iii) *The case without preferences.* If $\tilde p$ is flat
and $E$ uniform, $q(\pi) \propto e^{\gamma I_\pi(S; O)}$ — a pure explorer
that Gibbs-tilts by information gain.

### The closed loop and the information ceiling {#sec-fep-ceiling}

What Type III buys can be stated precisely with the ceiling of @sec-min-ceiling, which says that a self-referential training loop cannot
create information about the truth: if every update uses only the model's own
samples and a frozen equivalence relation, then
$I(\pi_T; a^\star \mid \pi_0, q, \sim) = 0$, and supervision breaks the chain
only because the verifier's reward makes the trained policy a function of the
answer as well. Active inference breaks the chain in the same way, and this
is, we think, the cleanest statement of what the closed loop is for. An
observation $o \sim p(o \mid s^\star, \pi)$ depends on the *true* hidden
state $s^\star$, so the agent's beliefs are not a function of themselves
alone. Moreover, if the agent's model is correct, the epistemic term
$I_\pi(S; O)$ is exactly the expected information, in nats, that the world
deposits into the beliefs under the policy $\pi$. The epistemic value of @eq-fep-efe therefore measures precisely the quantity that is missing from
the ceiling of @sec-min-ceiling.

The dividing line is then clear. The self-referential methods of @sec-min-entropy are open-loop, and their rewards come from the model itself;
perception and learning under the FEP are closed-loop and spend the incoming
information honestly at $T = 1$; and action of Type III goes out to acquire
it. The good regulator theorem of cybernetics says, as its title has it, that
every good regulator of a system must be a model of that system
[@conant1970good]; the closed loop is where that model is put to the test of
the world. Type III is also where the FEP meets the agents of the present:
the context acquisition of Dutta et al. (@sec-fep-ai), with inference inside
and the choice of data outside, is exactly the structure of @eq-fep-typeIII
[@dutta2026context], and among the objectives that the action–perception
divergence of Hafner et al. derives from one principle — representation
learning, information gain, empowerment, and skill discovery
[@hafner2020divergence] — information gain is the one that @eq-fep-typeIII
names.

### Self-referential tilts: learned preferences and habits {#sec-fep-selfref}

Two ingredients of the tilt @eq-fep-policy, the habits $E$ and the
preferences $\tilde p$, may themselves be learned from the agent's own
behaviour, and this is where the one failure mode of the chapter appears. We
observed in @sec-post-self that an external reward tilts the reference toward
what the world values, whereas an internal one tilts it toward what the model
already believes. Active inference has two places where an internal reward
can appear: habits, where $E$ reflects how often a policy has been chosen
before [@smith2022tutorial; @friston2016learning], and learned preferences,
where $\tilde p$ is estimated from experience [@sajid2021pepper]. The two
behave differently, and the difference is instructive.

::: {.callout-note title="Proposition 5 (critical precision for learned preferences)"}
Let there be $K$ actions, each deterministically yielding its own outcome, so
that $G(a) = -\log \tilde p(o_a)$ and $q(a) \propto \tilde p(o_a)^{\gamma}$.
Let the preferences have a fixed and a learned part,
$\tilde p = (1 - w)\, p + w\, u$ with $u$ uniform, where $p$ tracks the
agent's own outcomes, $p_{t+1} = (1 - \lambda)\, p_t + \lambda\, q_t$ for
$0 < \lambda \le 1$. Then i) $q$ minimizes
$\mathrm{KL}(q \Vert \tilde p) + (1 - 1/\gamma) H(q)$; and ii) the balanced
point $p = u$ is linearly stable if and only if $\gamma(1 - w) < 1$, i.e.,

$$
\gamma_c = \frac{1}{1 - w}, \qquad T_c = 1 - w ,
$$ {#eq-fep-gammac}

independently of $K$ and $\lambda$.
:::

Part i) follows because $q \propto \tilde p^{\gamma}$ minimizes
$\mathrm{CE}(q, \tilde p) - \gamma^{-1} H(q)$ and
$\mathrm{CE} = \mathrm{KL} + H$. For ii), put $p = u + \varepsilon$ with
$\sum_a \varepsilon_a = 0$; then $\tilde p = u + (1 - w)\varepsilon$, and to
first order $q_a = 1/K + \gamma(1 - w)\, \varepsilon_a$, so that
$\varepsilon_{t+1} = \big[1 - \lambda\big(1 - \gamma(1 - w)\big)\big]
\varepsilon_t$. The reading of i) is the point. At $\gamma = 1$ the objective
is pure fairness to the preferences and any $q = \tilde p$ is
self-consistent: this is the neutral point. For $\gamma > 1$ an entropy term
of positive weight $1 - 1/\gamma$ appears, which is minimum-entropy learning
at the level of policies, and if the preferences then follow the agent's own
behaviour, this is exactly the self-referential tilt of @sec-min-collapse.
With $w = 0$ the critical precision is $\gamma_c = 1$, the Bayesian value.

**Example 4 (learned preferences).** We take $K$ rooms, room 0 being dark,
and iterate the dynamics of Proposition 5. The numerics agree with @eq-fep-gammac: from a balanced start the symmetric state breaks at
$\gamma = 1.005$, $1.255$, and $2.005$ for $w = 0$, $0.2$, and $0.5$, on a
grid of step $0.005$, against the predicted $1$, $1.25$, and $2$. For
$w > 0$ the picture is that of @eq-min-selfconsistent. At $K = 2$ the
transition is continuous; for $K \ge 3$ a collapsed state reached from a
committed start remains stable below $\gamma_c$, giving a hysteresis window
— $[1.225, 1.25]$ and $[1.87, 2.0]$ at $K = 4$ for $w = 0.2$ and $0.5$ —
across which the largest probability jumps by about $0.49$ and $0.52$ (@fig-fep-preferences b): a continuous transition at $K = 2$ and a
first-order transition with hysteresis of mean-field Potts type for
$K \ge 3$ [@wu1982potts]. The case $w = 0$ is degenerate. The fixed points
of $p \mapsto p^{\gamma}/\sum_a p_a^{\gamma}$ are the distributions uniform
on a subset of the actions, since $p_a = p_a^{\gamma}/Z$ forces
$p_a^{\gamma - 1} = Z$ on the support; the balanced state loses stability at
$\gamma = 1$ exactly where the collapsed ones gain it, so the largest
probability jumps from $1/K$ to $1$ at $\gamma_c = 1$ for every $K$, with no
window. The time courses make it concrete. With $K = 4$, $w = 0$, and the
dark room ahead by 5 per cent,
$q_t(\text{dark})$ returns from $0.257$ to $0.250$ at $\gamma = 0.8$, stays
at $0.259$ at $\gamma = 1$, and rises to $0.994$ within 400 steps at
$\gamma = 1.25$ (@fig-fep-preferences a).

![Learned preferences as a self-referential tilt (Example 4). (a) Time courses of $q_t(\text{dark})$ for $K = 4$ and $w = 0$, with the dark room ahead by 5 per cent; (b) the resting value of the largest probability against the precision at $K = 4$, from a balanced start (solid) and a committed start (dashed), with $\gamma_c = 1/(1 - w)$ dotted and the hysteresis windows shaded. Produced by `code/fep-examples.py`.](../figures/fep-preferences.png){#fig-fep-preferences width="100%"}

So the dark room returns, but by a different door than the critics supposed.
Fixed preferences rule it out, as @tbl-fep-tmaze shows. Preferences learned
from one's own behaviour bring it back above a critical precision: the agent
learns to prefer what it happened to do more often, and then does it with
more confidence. Habits, by contrast, do not collapse in this way. If
$\tilde p$ is fixed and $E$ tracks past choices, then $q \propto E$ whenever
the policies have equal $G$, so $E$ enters the softmax with unit weight,
exactly at the neutral point — self-consistent but not amplifying. Collapse
requires the precision to amplify an internal reward beyond one. In both
cases it is the position of the precision relative to $T = 1$ that decides
whether a self-referential tilt keeps its diversity, which is the counterpart
of the critical value of @sec-min-collapse.

We should be plain about the status of this example. It is a toy model
constructed for this chapter, not a reproduction of any published agent; it
exhibits a possible failure mode, not an observed one.

### Schrödinger, steady states, and the maximum-entropy duality {#sec-fep-duality}

The reading of Schrödinger in @sec-min-schrodinger stresses that he describes
a stationary and fairly low entropy level — a balance, not a minimization —
and warns against transplanting thermodynamic theorems onto the Shannon
entropy of a predictive distribution. The entropic claim of @sec-fep-blankets
is compatible with that warning, provided it is read with the same care.

The claim is that the long-term average of surprise is an entropy, so that
minimizing free energy by selectively sampling the world bounds the entropy
of the sensory states [@friston2013life]. In the language of @sec-minimax-entropy the average surprise is a cross-entropy,
$\mathbb{E}_p[-\log p_m] = H(p) + \mathrm{KL}(p \Vert p_m) \ge H(p)$, which
is the identity behind the "closest to the truth" view, and which for a
maximum-entropy model at its maximum-likelihood fit also equals the model's
own entropy (@eq-max-bridge). Bounding the entropy therefore means that a
cross-entropy bounds the true entropy from above. It does not mean that
anything is pushed toward zero. And if the agent changes its sensory
distribution by acting, the first term of
$H(p^\pi) + \mathrm{KL}(p^\pi \Vert p_m)$ would reward the dark room — which
is exactly the term that the risk of @eq-fep-efe removes, as Example 2
showed.

The duality between the FEP and the constrained maximum entropy principle (@sec-fep-blankets) is where the physics of the FEP comes closest to this
book, since @sec-max-entropy is the maximum-entropy side of it
[@ramstead2023bayesian; @sakthivadivel2022geometry], and at the level of
paths the counterpart is the principle of maximum caliber
[@presse2013maxcal]. It is a conditional closeness, and the conditions are
under discussion (@sec-fep-critiques): it has been argued that the premises
of the blanket construction hold, even for linear stochastic systems, only
in a narrow region of parameter space [@aguilera2022particular], that
crucial steps of the original derivation needed assumptions that had not
been stated [@biehl2021critique], and that the relation between the
mathematical construct and the biological entities it is read onto needs
premises which the mathematics does not by itself supply
[@bruineberg2022emperor; @raja2021blanket; @colombo2021first]; the replies
and the later formulations are cited there. Whatever the outcome, we record
the Markov-blanket claims as *not derivable* from anything in this book:
they need assumptions about dynamics — a Langevin equation, sparse
coupling, a steady state — and about a partition, the Markov blanket, that
the book does not contain, and we would discourage the reader from treating
them as though they followed from it. The translations of @sec-fep-one to @sec-fep-selfref do not depend on them.

Two physical connections stand on firmer ground and deserve mention for that
reason. Still et al. show that the non-predictive information retained by a
stochastically driven system — the inefficiency of its implicit model — is
equivalent to thermodynamic dissipation, so that a system which keeps memory
about its environment and runs at maximal energetic efficiency must be
predictive [@still2012thermodynamics]. Ortega and Braun write
bounded-rational decision-making as a free energy trading expected utility
against information-processing cost measured in relative entropy
[@ortega2013thermodynamics]. The first gives prediction a thermodynamic
meaning that needs no Markov blanket; the second is the decision-theoretic
reading of the Gibbs tilts of @sec-max-entropy and @sec-post-training — a
free energy of the first kind, in the sense of @sec-fep-one.

### The correspondence at a glance {#sec-fep-corr}

The translations of this section are collected in @tbl-fep-corr, each with
its status.

| In the FEP | In this book | Status |
|------------------------------|----------------------------------------|----------------------|
| variational free energy $F[q; o]$ | @eq-max-def-free with $h = p(s)$, $T = 1$ | identity (Proposition 1) |
| perception: minimize $F$ over $q$ | inference over a maximum-entropy model, levels i)–ii) of @sec-max-definition | identity |
| precision of a Gaussian likelihood | temperature of the likelihood term | identity |
| predictive coding | the $T \to 0$ mode with a Laplace correction | approximation |
| learning (EM) | maximum-entropy learning with missing data; $T = 1$ on the dial of @sec-minimax-label-temperature; Type I on the completed data | identity (Proposition 2) |
| model evidence, complexity | Type I with a cost on the parameters; MDL, bits-back | correspondence |
| risk plus ambiguity | fairness to $\tilde p$ plus firmness (@sec-min-history) | identity (Proposition 3) |
| epistemic value | Type III (proposed); InfoMax; Lindley's information | new reading |
| $q(\pi) = \sigma(\log E - \gamma G)$ | the Gibbs tilts @eq-min-gibbs, @eq-post-tilt | identity (Proposition 4) |
| precision $\gamma$ | an inverse temperature that is inferred | correspondence |
| closed loop | breaks the information ceiling of @sec-min-ceiling | new reading |
| learned preferences, habits | self-referential tilt, @eq-min-selfconsistent | new (Proposition 5, Example 4) |
| average surprise bounds entropy | cross-entropy bounds entropy, the views of @sec-minimax-entropy | identity, with a caveat |
| Markov blankets, steady states | none; the maximum-entropy duality is the nearest point | not derivable |

: The correspondence between the free-energy principle and this book. {#tbl-fep-corr}

## Takeaway {#sec-fep-takeaway}

The principle itself can be summarized in three sentences. The FEP says that
a persisting system minimizes a variational bound on the surprise of its
sensations, by perception, by learning, and by action; active inference
scores actions by an expected free energy that combines a preference term
with an information-gain term and selects among them by a
precision-weighted softmax; and the physical claim that any system with a
Markov blanket does this is contested in detail, whereas the mathematics of
the first two sentences is not.


At its foundation, the translation is an exact identity.
The free energy of the FEP is
the free energy of this book at $T = 1$ (Proposition 1), and nearly
everything else follows from asking which base measure, which temperature,
and which outer problem is in force. Perception is inference over a
maximum-entropy model with no learner, and predictive coding is its
zero-temperature mode with a Laplace correction. Learning is maximum-entropy
learning with missing data, and its average free energy is the entropy of
the world model minus the entropy of the inferred causes (Proposition 2) —
Type I on the completed data, sitting at the $T = 1$ end of the dial of @sec-minimax-label-temperature rather than committing like Type II. Model
selection is Type I with a cost in nats. The posterior over policies is a
Gibbs tilt (Proposition 4), the same object as @eq-post-tilt with the
precision as an inverse temperature that is, unusually, inferred rather than
chosen. 
We note that the physics of Markov blankets and non-equilibrium steady states cannot be derived from the framework developed here.


Two things in the chapter are not translations. The first is Type III: the
expected free energy is firm but fair (Proposition 3) with the action, not
the classifier, as the optimized variable, and this is an outer problem the
book did not have — the one in which the data are not given but fetched (@tbl-fep-types). It is also what breaks the information ceiling of @sec-min-ceiling, since the epistemic value measures exactly the information
the world deposits into the beliefs. 
The second concerns the failure mode: when preferences are learned from one’s own predicted behaviour, setting the precision above its Bayesian value can re-open the dark room through a first-order transition (Proposition 5). This illustrates how the collapse mechanism described in @sec-min-collapse resurfaces within a theory that was originally intended to rule out such pathologies.


Significant open questions remain. The definition of expected free energy is not unique, and there is currently no consensus on a criterion for selecting among the various objectives proposed for this role [@millidge2021whence; @parr2019generalised; @champion2024reframing]. Whether recent approaches that recast planning as free-energy minimization within an expanded model framework [@devries2025efe; @nuijten2026efe] can provide such a criterion is, in our view, a key issue for future research.
Proposition 5 is proved for a model without hidden states, and the collapse
condition for learned preferences in a model that has them is unknown. Type
III invites a concrete programme for agents that acquire their own context
[@dutta2026context], where the question is whether the expected posterior
entropy of @eq-fep-typeIII is a usable objective at scale or merely a correct
one. And the label temperature of @eq-fep-learning-minimax still has no
schedule: this chapter shows that the FEP pins it at one, which is a
principled choice, but @sec-minimax-entropy leaves open whether anything
better is available when the goal is to commit.
